methodological_rigor.justification: This is a retrospective two-group comparison of prostate DWI sequences (48 SMS+SS-EPI vs 52 RS-EPI) with pathology from transperineal 12+X systematic plus targeted biopsy as the reference standard. The study specifies inclusion/exclusion criteria, obtains ethics approval, and uses blinded dual-reader subjective scoring with objective ROI-based metrics (SNR, CNR, contrast, ADC). However, sequence parameters differ materially between groups (e.g., FOV and matrix), and allocation to sequence is non-random, so confounding by protocol choice and imaging settings can influence both subjective quality and measured SNR/CNR. The statistical approach appears appropriate for group comparisons and ROC/AUC comparison (including a reported z-test), but details on inter-reader reliability and multiple-comparison control are not clearly presented in the excerpted text.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: The design is a single-center retrospective diagnostic-performance and technical comparison with an external reference (biopsy), aligning best with an Oxford LoE of 2b. The question is clinically relevant for prostate MRI workflows because DWI quality affects lesion detection and staging; the paper reports that RS-EPI improves distortion/sharpness while SMS+SS-EPI reduces acquisition time (1 min 50 s vs 3 min 43 s). Diagnostic performance based on ADC appears similar (AUC 0.925 vs 0.933; z=0.462, P=0.644), suggesting potential workflow gains without clear loss in ADC-based discrimination. Clinical applicability is moderate-high, though generalizability depends on scanner/protocol standardization and prospective confirmation.

reporting_quality.justification: Because the manuscript evaluates diagnostic efficacy using biopsy as the gold standard and reports ROC/AUC, STARD is the closest applicable reporting standard. The methods describe the reference standard, reader blinding, and key acquisition parameters for both sequences, and the abstract reports quantitative results with P-values and AUC comparison. At the same time, some STARD-relevant items are unclear from the provided text (patient flow details beyond exclusions, handling of indeterminate results, and full measures of reader agreement). There is no mention of data or code sharing beyond describing the scanner and workstation environment.

novelty_literature.justification: The work fills a practical gap by directly comparing SMS-accelerated SS-EPI with RS-EPI for prostate DWI, combining subjective quality assessment and ADC-based diagnostic performance against biopsy. The novelty is methodological/application-specific rather than conceptual, since both SMS acceleration and RS-EPI are established approaches in other anatomic settings. The key incremental contribution is the head-to-head clinical-protocol comparison and the tradeoff quantification between scan time, subjective fidelity, and ADC AUC. It is a useful extension but not a major departure from prior imaging optimization literature.

writing_presentation.justification: The abstract and methods are clear and quantitative, listing cohort sizes, endpoints, acquisition times, and the 5-point scoring rubric used by two blinded radiologists. Sequence parameters are provided in detail (TR/TE, echo gap, b-values, segmentation factor, SMS acceleration), enabling readers to understand protocol differences. The discussion appropriately interprets the subjective vs objective metric divergence and acknowledges limitations including small sample size and retrospective design. Overall readability is good with only minor awkward phrasing.

key_strengths: Uses biopsy as a reference standard and evaluates both subjective image quality and objective quantitative metrics (SNR/CNR/ADC) with blinded dual-reader scoring.
Reports a clear operational tradeoff: RS-EPI improves distortion/sharpness scores while SMS+SS-EPI markedly shortens scan time (1:50 vs 3:43) with similar ADC AUCs.
Provides detailed acquisition parameters for both sequences, supporting reproducibility of the technical comparison.
key_concerns: Retrospective non-randomized comparison with materially different protocol settings (e.g., FOV/matrix) introduces confounding that complicates attributing differences solely to sequence type.
Limited information on reader agreement statistics and multiplicity handling for multiple subjective/objective endpoints.
Single-center, short accrual window limits external generalizability across scanners, reconstruction pipelines, and PI-RADS workflows.
chief_reviewer.rationale: The paper provides clinically useful protocol-level evidence for sequence selection, but design and protocol confounding keep it from higher tiers; tightening reporting around agreement and controlling/standardizing parameters would strengthen the inference.
